owner: W1-17. RI-DLG01 §A — 'The player begins with exactly nine topics, granted at character creation.'
provenance: The nine keyword strings are community-data (the defaultTopics table in the Chargen Scenarios MWSE mod, cited by RI-DLG01 §Provenance). Every response text is ours.

key_legend.id: topic keyword slug; `name` is the keyword as the player sees it
key_legend.infos: the topic's INFO list, IN AUTHORED ORDER. First-match-wins: the engine returns the first entry whose WHOLE filter conjunction passes (RI-DLG01 §A).
key_legend.to: AddTopic edges. RI-DLG01 §A: 'The AddTopic calls in the result scripts are the edges of the graph.'
key_legend.cell: cell-name PREFIX match (filter field 6) — a settlement id here matches every cell inside it
key_legend.nj: [questId, op, value] journal condition that must NOT hold
key_legend.act: main-quest act gate, sugar for j on the main quest index
key_legend.q: true — this INFO is quest-bearing (it moves the journal)
key_legend.res: result script: {journal:[id,stage], flag:'name', modDisp:n, addTopic handled by `to`}

infos.x: The well is tended at dawn and again at the turn of the tide, and what is owed to it is counted twice. Once by the one who brings it. Once by the one who receives it. A thing given in the dark is not an offering, supplicant. It is a disposal. I have kept this well eleven years and I have never once counted alone.

If you are asking what I do here, provincial, the answer is that I hold an estate that the Empire says is not an estate. The duty is largely correspondence. Presumably you have better things to ask about.
I've no duties, dry-one. That's rather the difficulty with me. If I had one I'd keep it very carefully and I wouldn't let on that I had it. They'd take it back off me for a younger man.
Mine? Watch the wall. Count the boats. Write down what came off them. Half of it is lies. All of it goes in the manifest. Yours, citizen, I could not say.
This one buys. This one sells. Cart in the morning, cart at night. And it has been the same cart for nine years, friend.

In the strict sense my duty is the sequence: what arrived, in what order, and from whom. It is a smaller question than it sounds and a much larger one than the Office believes it is paying for. The catalogue runs three years behind, and the years it is behind are never the years anybody wants.
I was hatched at the third well and I was given to it before I was named. It is done less now than it was done then. The not-doing of it is one of the reasons the sap runs thin.
If you mean where I am from, provincial, the answer is a place that no longer sends me anything. If you mean what I am, that is a longer conversation and you have not earned it.

Yours or mine? Mine is a chapel school in Cyrodiil and twenty-one years of other people's paperwork, which is a background in the sense that a wall is a view. Yours the Office will have written down somewhere, and it will be wrong in one particular that you will never find out.
Chorrol. Second son. No land. So: the Cohort. Wet boots for twenty years, citizen, and I'm still here.
This one's mother pushed a cart. Her mother pushed a cart. Friend, you see the shape of it. Do you want the cart or the story?

Helstrom is not laid out, supplicant. It is grown. A place in it is described by which root you are standing under, not by which street you are on. Tell me what you are looking for and I will tell you the root.

There isn't much of Soulrest left to be specific about, dry-one. You want the salt pans, they're south past the dead well. You want the dead well, it's where they're all standing about not looking at it.
Name it and I will point. Stormhold is four streets and a wall. You cannot get lost. People do.
In Lilmoth? Ask which floor, friend. Half the doors are underwater. This one knows the dry ones.

Gideon is surveyed, which makes it the only settlement in the province I can describe without apologising. Fields to the west in a grid, timber yards on the river, the chapel on the only rise, and the inn where the survey pegs used to be. Ask for any of them by name.
There is the prison. There is the town that feeds it. That's Blackrose, citizen. Pick one!
Archon is the dye yards and the tide steps. Friend, follow your nose to the first one.
The hall. The gate. The needle-forest. Walk the boards, citizen. Not the ground.
Somewhere in the province, then. I can generally place a settlement to within a day's walk and a river to within the wrong bank. Name it and we will see which of us is more embarrassed.
Every person in Helstrom is written on the root they were given to. A name is not enough here, supplicant, and it never has been. Bring me the name and the well. I will bring you the person.
If the person is worth knowing, provincial, I already correspond with them. If they are not, I would not waste your time or, more to the point, mine.

I know most people by their boots, dry-one. It isn't as useless as you think. A man who's had the same boots resoled four times is staying. A man in new ones has just been paid for something. Yours are wrong for the water here, and I'd not say so to everyone.
This one knows every buyer. Friend, say a name. If they sell, this one knows them twice.
Ask at the muster board. Names, ranks, watches. If they are not on it, they are not ours. Then ask the Ledger.

The chapel keeps a roll of the tithed and the Office keeps a roll of the taxed, and the interesting people in Gideon are on precisely one of the two. Give me a name and I will tell you which roll it sits on. That will tell you rather more than the name did.

What is given at the well is not a service and it is not paid for. If you have come to buy healing you have come to the wrong root, supplicant. I would rather tell you now than let you be embarrassed in front of people. Ask me again when you have understood the difference.
Lilmoth sells everything twice. Once legally. Friend, this one can point at both counters.
Soulrest has a salt factor and a woman who sets bones, dry-one. The salt factor won't see you and the bone-setter will. Between them, there's nothing else this place can still do for a person.
Cohort quartermaster for arms. Ledger house for coin. Physician on the wall street. Nothing here is cheap, citizen.

Gideon has an inn, a chapel, a timber factor and a smith who is better than the town deserves. It also has an Office annexe that will sell you a copy of any document you can name, and several you cannot. That is more service than anywhere else in the province, and Gideon is quietly insufferable about it. I have lived here nine years and caught it myself.
This one has a cart. That is a service. Friend, what do you need moved?
It is not a trade, supplicant. It is an obligation that is inherited, and the difference is that a trade may be put down.
Administration, of an estate whose legality is a matter of opinion. If you want the opinion, provincial, read the treaty. If you want the estate, take it up with the Empire.

I ask, dry-one. It's a trade like any other, in that most of the day goes on walking to where the customers are. It's unlike any other in one particular. The customers would rather I wasn't there when I arrive.
Sap. Salt. Dye. Whatever weighs less than it sells for. This one does not ask where a bundle slept.

Records, which is not a trade so much as an accusation people make about me. In practice it is reconciliation: two documents about the same barge, disagreeing, and then a decision about which one the Empire will believe for the next thirty years. I make that decision, and nobody has ever asked me how.
Soldiering. Nine years of it here. The trade is standing still. Everything else is training.
Don't put your hands in the dye vats, dry-one. Not even to point at something. The colour doesn't come off for a season, and the guards in Archon read a purple hand as a confession.

Advice is given to those who intend to take it. So I will give you the one thing that is not advice but law. What is drawn from a well is returned to a well. The province is not interested in whether you knew, supplicant, and neither am I.
Should you wish to survive the interior, provincial, do not accept water. Everything else you will work out or you will not.
Do not draw in the street. Do not argue with a writ. Pay the gate fee. It is smaller than the fine.
Lilmoth advice? Never take the low stair at high water. Friend, this one has seen it close.

Carry a written thing with a seal on it. It need not be relevant. The Cohort cannot read the interior dialect of Imperial legal hand, and the assumption that a sealed document must be important survives contact with the evidence remarkably well. I keep three such things about me and none of them are mine.
Walk the boards. Trust the boards. Friend, the ground here isn't ground!

topics.name: latest rumors

infos.x: I do not repeat rumour on principle, which is a principle I hold for about as long as it takes to be asked a second time. Ask in the street. They will have the same story I have, and they will tell it faster, and three of them will tell it wrong.

topics.note: The rumour POOL itself is game/data/dialogue/rumours/*.json, partitioned per settlement and per main-quest act. This INFO is the last-resort catch-all for a speaker who has no rumour pool entry that passes — RI-DLG01's Greeting-9 discipline applied to a topic.

infos.x: For you? This one will say it once. The Ledger weighs sap wet. Friend, that is a whole cart in ten.
Quietly, then. Half the muster is names. Dead men, drawing pay. The paymaster knows. So does the tribune.

There is a well that is not on the rolls. It is not tended and it has not gone quiet. The keeper who found it decided the covenant was better served by a lie than by a procession, and she kept it off the rolls herself. I have carried that forty years, supplicant. I still do not know whether she was right.
Since you have been useful: the treaty has a clause about heirs. It has not been read in ninety years. I have read it.

Very well, and this does not leave the room. The survey of the eastern rootlands was never completed, and the reason given in the file is weather. The reason in the surveyor's own hand, on the back of the last sheet, is that the party was told to stop. The man who ordered it has had his name scraped off the paper with a knife. I have asked for that sheet twice and I have stopped asking.

You've been kind to me and I'll be kind back, dry-one. The man they fished out of the cut in the spring didn't drown. I saw him walk down to the water on his own feet. There was a man behind him who wasn't hurrying. I've told nobody and I'm not going to.
A secret? Friend, this one sells those. Come back when we are better acquainted.
